slides.label: Exercises for Act III
slides.notes: Open by reframing the chapter as a diagnostic lab for the whole curvature act. The exercises are not a loose problem list; they are a sequence of tests that ask whether a learner can attach a measurement to the correct geometric object and then check whether the expected invariant survives representation changes.

slides.label: From Problems To Probes
slides.notes: Use the dashboard as the route for the lecture. Each checkpoint has the same grammar: build an object, measure a curvature or topological quantity, perturb the representation, and verify what remains stable. This gives students a strategy for reading every Act III exercise without copying any exercise statement.

slides.label: Curve Curvature As A Sampling Test
slides.notes: The first diagnostic separates the curve from its parameterization. A reliable computation samples position, velocity, and acceleration, but the inspected quantity is the signed turning per unit arclength. Ask students to predict what should change under resampling and what should remain the same.

slides.label: Frenet Frame And Torsion Lab
slides.notes: The helix turns curve exercises into a controlled experiment because it has exact nonzero targets for both curvature and torsion. The instructor should treat the moving frame as the visible object and the two constants as calibration readings: if either drifts under uniform sampling, the computation is suspect.

slides.label: Surface Curvature Gallery
slides.notes: This slide shifts from curves to surfaces by asking students to classify local bending before computing. The gallery separates positive, zero, and negative Gaussian curvature. The goal is not to memorize shapes; it is to connect the sign of the product of principal curvatures with what crosses or stays on one side of the tangent plane.

slides.label: Shape Operator Coordinate Check
slides.notes: The shape-operator slide is the main representation test. Principal coordinates diagonalize the operator, while a rotated basis usually introduces off-diagonal terms. The trace, determinant, and eigenvalues should agree across both views, so the exercise becomes a check that the operator is geometric rather than a coordinate artifact.

slides.label: Gauss-Bonnet Ledger
slides.notes: Use the ledger to make global curvature accounting concrete. Local curvature, corner turns, boundary turning, and topology are not separate facts; they are entries in one conservation statement. The table lets students see Euler characteristic as the number that predicts the total curvature budget.

slides.label: Vector Field Index
slides.notes: Poincare-Hopf is the topology counterpart to Gauss-Bonnet in this review. Instead of integrating curvature, we add turning numbers around zeros of a vector field. The diagnostic is the same: local measurements are allowed to move under deformation, but their total has to match the Euler characteristic.

slides.label: Curvature Exercise Playbook
slides.notes: Close by giving students a repeatable playbook. Every exercise should be read as an audit: identify the object, name the measurement, choose the invariant, and state the common pitfall. The chapter has done its job when learners can design those checks before they start calculating.
